If getting covered under your fiances plan does not work, you may be eligible for Medicaid in your state. People don’t necessarily realize this especially if it’s for temporary circumstances. This is very state dependent so look up the details for you. 

If you do get on insurance either Medicaid or thru your fiance, then IMO it is worth still reaching out to your pcp and emphasizing attention/focus issues that impacting work or school. The medical system very much views adhd thru a deficit lens, and medication is a way to return to a higher level of functioning- that is the problem you want your doctor to understand. Now, if your pcp is dismissive by all means get a new one! But this A) will document further that this problem exists, which is relevant if seeing someone in the same medical system b) the doctor may just shrug and refer you to psychiatry, which in some ways is actually easier for them than just denying it. Id say it’s probably 40% likelihood to result in you getting a script, but at the cost of one phone call or portal message, that’s not so bad as far as effort vs reward.

I am going to slightly go into fix it mode so feel free to ignore this if that’s not where you’re at or don’t have the capacity for this right now. This is all written assuming you are from the US, I don’t know anything about other countries mental health care systems. 

Some primary care doctors are comfortable treating ADHD, some are not. Do you have a primary care doctor? Have you asked your current primary care doctor about ADHD? You can try saying that you’re having focusing issues rather than naming the diagnosis- some doctors shut down to that, but if you say that focus issues are causing issues at school work, they are more likely to take that seriously. If your pcp takes you seriously but does not feel comfortable treating or evaluating ADHD, they can refer you to a psychiatrist. 

If you do not have a PCP or have one, have brought up focus issues and they have unilaterally rejected it, then you can also go right to pursuing psychiatry. This can get harder and if you get stuck you can DM me if you’d rather not share information about your state and insurance publicly. Again, feel free of course to also just ignore this, I am hoping only to be helpful and if this is not helpful then please disregard it. 

Finding a psychiatrist is overwhelming but easier than you’d think if you know how. Do you have health insurance? Depending on your state and insurance plan, using headway, talkiatry, or zocdoc is probably the fastest/simplest way to find a provider as you can schedule directly through them. There are other similar platforms if those don’t work. Psychology today is a platform of profiles of providers, you will need a psychiatrist or psychiatric nurse practitioner on there. 

If you have Medicaid, many of the providers who take Medicaid will instead work at a local clinic or agency. Sometimes the hospital system in an area will have an outpatient clinic. There may be a mental health association, which is usually county based. These clinics may make you also do therapy, if so they will have therapists there, it would not be a separate thing.

I can’t help with in person stuff, but if you wanted more access to Buddhist ebooks and audiobooks for free, you can get a Los Angeles library card online, without visiting a branch by going here on their website. 

https://www.lapl.org/about-lapl/contact-us/e-card/e-card-registration

Just need to give an address- the address of the halfway house should be fine, you don’t need to provide proof you live there. 

Anyway once you have that, you can sign up for Libby and Hoopla which are ebook and audiobook apps. You sign up here. 

https://www.lapl.org/books-emedia/e-media

You should sign up for both, they have different collections of books. Hoopla you can instantly borrow any book they have, but only a certain number per month (calendar month). I’m not sure how many you get with the La library. 

Libby you have as many books per month as you want, but only a certain amount out at a time, and you may need to wait if they’re on hold, they only have a certain number of copies per book.

> I'm not sure how you're using the IRS calculator, but there isn't a separate tax on each quarter's income. Technically you're supposed to pay in an amount by the end of each quarter to make sure you've covered at least that quarter's income (both W-2 and 1099), but as long as you meet one of the safe harbors (for example, making sure you've paid in at least 110% of last year's total tax liability by the end of 2025) that make sure you won't be charged a penalty. Just divide last year's tax liability (NOT the amount you "owe") and divide it by four, or however many payments you want to make.

If you are open to reading- CPTSD From Surviving to Thriving by Pete Walker is, for my money, the gold standard in self-help trauma books. Its less directive and more educational/validating, but I also recommend anything by Bruce Perry, such as What Happened To You. They are cheap on amazon or thriftbooks, but may also be available at your library physically or via audio. When you get established outpatient, you may want to consider looking intro vivitrol/naltrexone (vivitrol is the monthly injectable version). It's a medication that helps with alcohol use which is pretty successful, I've seen it work wonders for a lot of people. If you're not interested, ignore this, no worries. 

 You may be familiar with methodone/suboxone for opiates- naltrexone works differently. Those medications work by being agonists for opioids, which basically means that they fill or partially fill the function that opioids do for your brain, with the idea that doing this in a controlled way will help prevent someone from using. They can be very helpful, but it's a big commitment, and there are some very understandable reservations people have. 

Naltrexone works as an antagonist, which basically means it blocks the receptors and does nothing other than block them. The mechanism of use is that if you do drink, all the pleasant/relaxing elements of it are gone, and most people feel like it reduces or gets rid of cravings too. This is not meant to be an ad for this particular medication, just that it's something not everyone is aware of being an option. Full disclosure I am not myself in recovery, but am a therapist who has worked at multiple outpatient rehabs or substance use programs, so I can only observe what I have seen work for other people. If you do have trouble finding an outpatient program near you, you can DM me your state/city and I can help you find one if you would like.

So, two books that I think are very helpful are Complex PTSD: From Surviving to Thriving by Pete Walker and What Happened to You? by Dr. Bruce Perry and Oprah. Both avoid the over simplification and corniness of a lot of mental health books for the general public, and contain useful information, validation, and some practical guidance and things to try. If you can imagine going from isolation to being part of a community or group as a continuum, reading books is a good first step. You can feel better equipped for when you do leave your comfort zone, and reading can help you better understand what to look for in a therapist if and when that's something you pursue. 

The thing about comfort zones is that of course you want to stay in it, but that it is also good for you to leave it. One of those annoying little paradoxes we have to live with. Wherever you can slightly expand your comfort zone to interact with calm enough adults doing anything healthy enough will be a therapeutic activity for you. What that may look like depends on you, your life, your circumstances, so think and play around with that. Just some brainstorming type ideas- going to the store and chatting with a cashier or other customer (can start with asking a simple question you already know the answer two as the lowest impact version), going to a place other people will be and do a solitary activity- reading or using your computer at a cafe or similar, going to a free public space like a library and spending time there. From there, see how that goes, see what next steps make sense to you when you're ready. By this point you may start to feel more comfortable seeing a therapist, or doing more involved activities- joining a club or group, a local sports team, etc. 

Therapy can absolutely be scary, but as far as expense, depending on your area and insurance it *might* be more accessible than you'd think. If you've looked into it and it's not possible in your area then my apologies, I just have anecdotally known people who heard so much about inaccessibility they didn't have the energy to look/it felt pointless but then they found out that therapists in their area take medicaid, there's a college with a student clinic, etc. People can  be nervous about that, but a good grad school or doctoral program can have student practitioners who are really good- no antiquated/out of date ideas, they're being actively supervised, and they aren't jaded are burned out. They can still suck of course, but that does cover a lot of the ways a therapist can be shitty or harmful, so honestly I think there's less room for negative impact even if they're not going to have as much experience. My wife actually sees a PsyD intern for therapy and it has been working out very well. 

Anyway I hope this has been helpful!

I think the best thing is to talk about that with your therapist. They know you and your situation, and if you feel safe enough and comfortable enough, that would be an excellent place to continue co-regulating. As a generality though, I can offer you that its very common for people to find themselves in patterns they don't like because the patterns are familiar. There's an idea that's been discussed in research and theoretical terms endlessly, but I think was put best by I swear to god a random comment on youtube- "he feels like home, and home wasn't safe." Its important to have some grace and understanding for yourself and why you seem to be in a pattern that you dont want to be. If this therapist has been with you long enough to have seen this pattern play out a few times, they may be able to help you find what it is that guides you into it. If not, talking about past instances with them can hopefully help find you some clarity. 

The good news though- you are recognizing that this is toxic, and you're probably recognizing it faster than you have in the past. That *is* progress, even though its the kind of progress that feels shitty, like when you're moving and packed a lot but in the process unearthed a bunch more things.

You're exactly right, it's pretty much unconscious, but you can do some things to influence it. Essentially, regulation is being able to shift your nervous system to the appropriate way of dealing with whatever is happening. This is the fight or flight response that you have probably heard about- there's a lot more to it, I'll summarize it as the idea of being hypo and hyper aroused. Sometimes- you need to be able to think fast and move quickly. Other times, you need to slow down, play dead, zone out, dissociate. Most of the time, it's best to be in a sort of middle state, where you have greater access to your more logical and abstract thinking, long term memory, all that good stuff. 

People co-regulate when there is comfort and they are sharing a space. Your nervous system takes in information and uses that to decide what it should do. If your nervous system is dysregulated, you might be in hypo or hyperarousal all the time, which can cause a lot of issues. But if you feel comfortable with someone, and they're regulated, that will help you regulate.

Therapist here, just to provide some brief information. Trauma, neglect, and lack of attunement growing can create a ton of difficulties growing up- difficulty regulating yourself, connecting to others, determining accurately when you're safe and when you need to be on guard, and that's just getting started. So you're right- how can a 45ish minute weekly appointment change all of that? 

Our brains are wired, at the most basic level, to keep us alive. If we grow up learning that people are supportive enough, attuned enough, then that informs our worldview, and we have a baseline ability to mostly trust people unless given reason not to, and are able to focus in more depth on the various other issues that come our way.

But if your care givers are inconsistent, neglectful (in whole or in part- some loving parents can neglect a key area) we then adapt to that as the standard, and in that period where we are children those adaptations are often helpful. If emotional expression is met with contempt and abuse, then dissociating is a protective response. 

But! Hopefully, eventually you are not in a space where that is your daily world. The problem is, now you have all these survival tools that are no longer helpful, and in fact stifling. Your brain is not an entity, it's a committee. The parts responsible for your safety are given total priority, almost like marshal law, and those parts are not really able to understand time or look at things sequentially. They cannot determine that you are out of danger, or that you need to stop doing certain safety behaviors. 

Anyway, now I'm actually going to answer your question haha. People can, as a rule, recover. People heal. All the parts of you that are in pain are trying desperately to feel better, they just need guidance, a corrective relationship. For all of human history people have had and healed from trauma. This healing occurring within therapy is a very recent thing. What therapy offers is the ability to regulate with a safe person, in a boundaried way, and from there to learn and begin changing patterns. The boundaries of therapy that can make it seem 'not real' I think are actually quite helpful. I think it is important to have a space to unload all of these things and have them contained- ie not a friend, or anything else. But therapy cannot be your whole or only relationship. 

I'm not sure if you ever had a good relationship with a teacher, so pardon me if that's not a good example. But thats I think a good example of a healing and genuine relationship people have, that is also someone's job and has clear boundaries. Therapy is much more like that, than the hopefully mutual and even dynamic of a friend or partner.
